source: Uzzi, Mukherjee, Stringer, Jones (2013) Atypical combinations and scientific impact. Science 342:468-472
finding: Read the paper text. Hit = top 5% of citations. Papers mixing mostly conventional journal pairs with a tail of atypical pairs were hits nearly twice as often as the 5% background. Atypical-only or conventional-only papers were near background or below.
numbers: 17.9M WoS papers. Top-5% hit rate per 100 papers: high median conventionality + high tail novelty 9.11; high conventionality + low tail novelty 5.82; low conventionality + high tail novelty 5.33; low + low 2.05; background 5. Differences P<0.00001. Teams 37.7% more likely than solo authors to insert novel combinations. Tail novelty = 10th-percentile z-score below 0; about 40.8% (1980s) and 40.7% (1990s) of papers per the working-paper version. Same pattern for top 1% and top 10% hits and in 243 fields.
quote: papers with an injection of novelty into an otherwise exceptionally familiar mass of prior work are unusually likely to have high impact
limits: Observational, citation-based, journal-pair proxy for combination. Citations are not validity. Replication with newer data not found this session (search quota gone).
agent_relevance: Design rule: mostly conventional base plus one or few atypical inserts, not all-far. Fits O7 as a bounded far insertion into a conventional frame.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Re-ran Webb et al. letter-string analogies with permuted alphabets and symbol alphabets. Prolific humans stay steady; GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 drop as the alphabet is permuted more. Comprehension checks show the models understand the new alphabets (GPT-4 successor check 0.76-1.00), so the drop is not simple misreading.
numbers: 136 Prolific participants (some rejected), 14 problems each. GPT-3 davinci-003, GPT-3.5-turbo-0613, GPT-4, temperature 0. Share of errors that follow an alternate rule: 5.81% GPT-3, 22% GPT-4, 38.59% humans. Per-condition model accuracies are in figures only.
limits: Letter-string family only. No Claude and no reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Do not trust an LLM analogy score on familiar forms. Test any O7 mapping step on counterfactual items. Gap 9 answered for GPT-4 only.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Extended the test to digit matrices and story analogies. Humans hold up on variants; GPT models fall on most. For stories GPT-4 is biased by answer order and sensitive to paraphrase of the correct target.
numbers: From Webb et al. data: GPT-4 on 18 story problems scored 89% (16/18) when Story A was correct but 61% (11/18) when Story B was correct. 245 human participants for stories, 6 problems each. Letter-string table for GPT-3.5 by number of generalisations 0 to 3: 0.488, 0.358, 0.317, 0.160 (table partly garbled in text).
limits: GPT-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 (0613) only. 18 story items, probably in pretraining data.
agent_relevance: Far-story matching is brittle to order and surface paraphrase. Randomise candidate order and test a paraphrase before trusting a match.

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN: Analogical Reasoning on Narratives
finding: Tests whether LLMs find system (relational) analogies between narratives when the near distractor shares only surface features. Humans are near ceiling. Models are much worse on FAR analogies, and GPT-4 is below random there.
numbers: Binary choice, random baseline 50%. Overall models 57% vs humans 96%. Near analogies: models 75.0%, humans 97.9%. Far analogies: models average 39.6% (below random), humans 94.1%. GPT-4 close to humans on near, below random on far.
limits: Mainly GPT-3.5 with GPT-4 in few-shot; no reasoning models. Narrative form, not code or design.
agent_relevance: Picking a far analogue by surface-vs-structure judgment fails. Verify by execution (supports K03, K05).

source: Stevenson et al. (2023) Do large language models solve verbal analogies like children do?
finding: Six Dutch and multilingual LLMs solve children's A:B::C:? analogies at about child level. With associative shortcuts controlled, each model drops 1-2 age years. Correct answers often come from association with C.
numbers: 14,006 children aged 7-12 solved 622 Dutch analogies. Best models (GPT-3, XLM-V) slightly above the 11-year-old level; M-GPT around age 7. Drop 1-2 years under control.
limits: Word-level analogies in Dutch, older models.
agent_relevance: High word-analogy scores can come from association. Use relation-controlled items when testing the abstraction step.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Nova: iterative planning and search to enhance novelty and diversity of LLM ideas
finding: Planned iterative retrieval raises the count of unique novel ideas 3.4 times over no-planning. Ablation: removing retrieval or planning lowers unique ideas. No continued gain after about 3 rounds.
numbers: 170 seed papers; 3 iterations; Swiss Tournament top-rated ideas at least 2.5 times more than Si et al., AI-Scientist and ResearchAgent; 3.4x unique novel ideas. Ablation values figure-only.
limits: Novelty by embedding similarity, Claude Sonnet ranker and a human check; no execution. Sources are topic-relevant, not deliberately far. Not equal-token.
agent_relevance: Nearest evidence for gap 6: iteration gains that saturate near 3 rounds. Distance not varied and tokens not matched.

source: Kumar et al. (2024) Can LLMs unlock novel scientific research ideas?
finding: Four LLMs (Claude-2, Gemini-1.0, GPT-3.5, GPT-4) write future-work ideas for papers in five fields. Retrieved background (RAG over 190K CS abstracts, top 20) is added in one condition. Scored by IAScore (match to authors' ideas) and a distinctness index. Many ideas are generic.
numbers: Physics human review of 630 ideas over 63 papers: Claude 15.28% non-novel, 16.02% generic, 31.22% moderate, 20.36% very novel, 17.12% extremely novel; GPT-4 7.33%, 14.53%, 42.22%, 28.0%, 7.95%. CS: 76.67% of Claude ideas rated relevant. Ideas of 20-40 words score highest on IAScore.
limits: Matching authors' future work is a similarity score, not validity. Retrieval is near. No equal-token control.
agent_relevance: Another similarity-scored result. Do not treat IAScore-like measures as proof a combination is valid.

source: Hope et al. (2017) Accelerating innovation through analogy mining (KDD)
finding: Re-read the user study. Purpose/mechanism representations retrieve analogies that lead to more ideas rated good. Purpose-only and mechanism-only versions also beat TF-IDF in the retrieval table.
numbers: Within-subjects ideation. P(good idea), k=2 judges: ours 0.71 [0.48, 0.87], TF-IDF 0.28 [0.16, 0.44], random 0.27 [0.16, 0.41]. k=3: ours 0.56 [0.36, 0.75], TF-IDF 0.16 [0.08, 0.27], random 0.14 [0.08, 0.24]. A coefficient B=-1.94 (p<.01) is printed for k=3; k=2 B=-1.81 vs TF-IDF per critique. Judge kappa 0.51. Mixed-model AIC 682.28 to 620.32.
limits: Single small study, product corpus, authors' own method vs weak baselines, kappa 0.51. No independent replication found.
agent_relevance: Large but unreplicated. Gap 5 independent replication stays open; see d09 for the same group's follow-up.

source: Hope et al. (2022) Scaling creative inspiration with fine-grained functional aspects of ideas (CHI)
finding: Same group rebuilds the purpose/mechanism idea with a neural span extractor, so no hand annotation at run time. On a new corpus, aspect-based retrieval beats strong embedding baselines for alternative uses and design-space inspirations. This is an extension by overlapping authors, not an independent replication.
numbers: Span extraction GCN F1 about 48%. Alternative-uses search MAP 87% (baselines 40-60%). 10 raters, 2584 boxes (12,920 purpose descriptors): 51% of inspirations rated useful by at least 2 raters vs best baseline under 30%; 62% of boxes had at least 2 useful vs 39% best baseline. Relative boost 50-60%.
quote: Achieving abstraction to match across distant domains ... remains an open problem
limits: Aspects stay close to surface text; raters are engineers; usefulness ratings, not outcomes.
agent_relevance: A learned purpose/mechanism index reproduces the direction of the 2017 effect at near-to-medium distance. Far transfer still open.

source: Meyerson, Lehman et al. (2023) Language model crossover: variation through few-shot prompting
finding: LLM acts as the crossover operator over parent strings, equations and programs. Validity is checkable by parsing and fitness, so no LLM judge is needed. More parents in the prompt gives more diverse offspring. Bigger LLM gives more valid offspring.
numbers: Sodarace: roughly 30% of offspring valid with the 6B model; more parents raise niches filled and QD score; one parent acts as plain mutation. One-point crossover is a strong baseline for symbolic regression (statistically similar to LMX with no header).
limits: Parents are in-domain solutions, not far-domain sources. Small 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Combination can be scored by validity and fitness (gap 8). Keep a plain crossover baseline.

source: Novikov et al. (2025) AlphaEvolve: a coding agent for scientific and algorithmic discovery
finding: Programs scored by automatic evaluators. Ablations on tensor decomposition and kissing numbers: no evolution (same initial program fed repeatedly), no prompt context, small base LLM only, no meta-prompt evolution, no full-file evolution each give a worse target metric at equal compute budget.
numbers: Three seeds per setting; curves averaged over targets with intra-target SD. Exact values figure-only.
limits: Sources are earlier programs from the same task archive, not far domains. Needs an automatic evaluator.
agent_relevance: At equal compute, building on an archive beats repeated fresh sampling when the score is executable (indirect evidence for gaps 2 and 6 in code). Distance not tested.

source: Lange et al. (2025) ShinkaEvolve: open-ended and sample-efficient program evolution
finding: Execution-scored evolution with archive inspiration programs, crossover mutation and novelty rejection sampling (reject if code embedding similarity above 0.95). Ablations: weighted parent selection beats best-of-N and hill climbing; embedding rejection beats no rejection; an added LLM novelty judge gives marginal gain.
numbers: Circle packing, state of the art with 150 evaluations. Ablation curves vs number of LLM proposals are figure-only. Default top-k inspirations = 2.
limits: No ablation of inspirations or crossover alone. Inspirations are in-task.
agent_relevance: A cheap embedding filter against near-copies lifted score at equal proposal count (gap 10, partly). Forced distance not tested.

source: Li et al. (2024) Chain of Ideas: novel idea development with LLM agents
finding: Organising retrieved literature as a progressive chain, rather than mixing papers into the prompt, is the largest contributor in an LLM-judged ablation. Removing future-trend prediction lowers novelty; removing entities lowers clarity and effectiveness.
numbers: Pairwise vs full agent, 50 matches, 50 = tie. Without chain: novelty 41, significance 39, clarity 44, feasibility 49, effectiveness 39, average 42.4. Without future trend: average 46.2. Without entities: average 45.4.
limits: LLM judge only (see K13). Topic-near retrieval. Extra stages mean not equal-token.
agent_relevance: Structure of retrieved sources matters more than mere inclusion. Supports an explicit organise step, says nothing on distance.

source: Si et al. (2025) The ideation-execution gap
finding: Opened the paper to check gap 8. Execution of ideas by experts is the strongest validity check found: LLM idea scores fall more than human ones after execution, erasing the novelty edge.
numbers: Figures as in a12/c05: novelty change -1.049 vs -0.010; overall -1.976 vs -0.628. Full-text tables not re-extracted this session.
limits: Human execution is too costly for an agent loop. Same group as Si 2024.
agent_relevance: Validity must be tested by running things. Code or test execution is the affordable analogue.

source: Gap-search record: web search quota exhausted; arXiv API, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar rate-limited
finding: Searches for far-vs-near ablation at equal tokens, abstraction-first vs more samples, an inverted U in source distance for LLMs, Gu et al. replication with matched references, Claude and reasoning-model counterfactual analogy tests, Chan-Schunn iteration for LLM agents, and source forcing vs diversity could not be run. Papers were reached by known arXiv id only.
numbers: No new studies found for gaps 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 (LLM-agent version), 9 (Claude and reasoning models), 10.
limits: Absence reflects the search limit, not proof that no study exists.
agent_relevance: These stay open. Treat as experiments for our own harness.

source: Gu et al. (2024) LLMs can realize combinatorial creativity (re-checked for gaps 3-4)
finding: Searched the full PDF text (about 250k characters) for ablations, a baseline with matched references, a judge and variance. The only comparison is a baseline that generates directly from the problem statement without multi-level retrieval, scored by embedding similarity. No ablation of L1-L4 found.
numbers: As c01: SPECTER cosine 0.85 vs 0.78 (design rationale), 0.83 vs 0.75 (universal principles), 0.87 vs 0.77 (key mechanisms); 87 papers.
limits: Text search by keyword only; the word ablation did not occur in the method or results.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 4 stay open. Treat as a design, not a result.
